title: The Controlled Substances Act, Marijuana and Schedule I
h1: The Controlled Substances Act: How Marijuana Landed in Schedule I and What's Changing
metaDescription: How the 1970 Controlled Substances Act put marijuana in Schedule I, what the 1972 Shafer Commission advised and where rescheduling stands as of October 2026.
excerpt: A plain-language guide to the 1970 federal law behind cannabis policy: the five schedules, the 1972 commission report and what rescheduling means for Michigan now.
keyTakeaways: Congress wrote marijuana into Schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act, signed October 27, 1970.
A national commission appointed by President Nixon advised in 1972 against criminal penalties for personal use; his administration didn't follow it.
Since April 28, 2026, marijuana under a state medical license is in Schedule III; adult-use marijuana is still Schedule I.
As of October 2026, a broader rescheduling proposal was still awaiting a judge's recommended decision.
body:
When the Controlled Substances Act was signed in 1970, it put marijuana in Schedule I, the strictest federal category, and adult-use marijuana is still there. That listing still shapes cannabis in Michigan, from how dispensaries are taxed to why you shouldn't carry cannabis across state lines. Here's how the law works and what has changed as of October 2026.

## What the Controlled Substances Act does

President Nixon signed the act on October 27, 1970, as part of a larger federal drug law. It sorts drugs into five schedules and ties federal controls and penalties to each one. States can legalize cannabis under their own laws, but they can't change the federal list, and that gap explains a lot.

## The five schedules and what they mean

The statute sets three findings for each schedule. The first two are always potential for misuse and accepted medical use in this country. The third is a lack of accepted safety under medical supervision for Schedule I and the risk of dependence for the rest.

| Schedule | Potential for misuse | Accepted medical use? | Third finding |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | High | No | Lacks accepted safety even under medical supervision |
| II | High | Yes, sometimes with severe restrictions | Dependence can be severe |
| III | Lower than I and II | Yes | Moderate or low physical, or high psychological, dependence |
| IV | Low compared with III | Yes | Limited dependence compared with III |
| V | Low compared with IV | Yes | Limited dependence compared with IV |

The original lists put heroin and LSD in Schedule I and cocaine in Schedule II.

## 1970: the Controlled Substances Act, marijuana and Schedule I

Congress listed marijuana in Schedule I in the text of the law itself, so federal law regarded the plant as having a high potential for misuse and no accepted medical use. Changing that takes new legislation or a formal federal rescheduling process, and marijuana stayed in Schedule I for more than five decades.

## The 1972 commission report and why its advice went unheeded

President Nixon appointed the National Commission on Marihuana and Drug Abuse, known as the Shafer Commission after its chairman, Raymond P. Shafer. Its 1972 report, *Marihuana: A Signal of Misunderstanding*, recommended moving away from criminal penalties for personal use and discouraging use in other ways.

The administration didn't follow it. The report landed less than a year after the President called drug abuse "public enemy number one," and policy kept moving toward enforcement. Our [War on Drugs history](/blog/war-on-drugs-cannabis-history/) picks up from there, and our look at [anti-cannabis propaganda](/blog/anti-cannabis-propaganda-history/) covers the messaging.

## Decades of consequences: arrests, research limits, banking and tax rules

- **Arrests:** at the peak, hundreds of thousands of marijuana arrests a year.
- **Research:** Schedule I research runs under its own federal rules, and researchers have said those restrictions kept potent legal-market products out of their studies.
- **Taxes:** Section 280E of the tax code bars businesses trafficking in Schedule I or II substances from deducting normal expenses.
- **Banking:** because federal law still prohibits most marijuana sales, banks that serve cannabis businesses take on extra federal reporting duties, even for state-licensed stores.
- **Borders:** federal law applies across state lines and on federal land.

## States go their own way: medical and adult-use laws, Michigan included

Michigan voters approved a medical marijuana program in 2008 and adult-use legalization in 2018, and the state's Cannabis Regulatory Agency licenses the businesses. Our [Michigan cannabis law guide](/cannabis-laws-by-state/michigan/) covers the state's requirements, and our [hemp vs. marijuana explainer](/blog/hemp-vs-marijuana-difference/) shows why hemp follows a separate federal track.

## Rescheduling: what has happened and what it would change

1. **October 2022:** the President asked federal officials to review marijuana's scheduling.
2. **August 2023:** federal health officials recommended Schedule III.
3. **May 2024:** the Justice Department proposed Schedule III.
4. **April 28, 2026:** a final federal order moved marijuana covered by a state medical license, and marijuana drugs approved by the FDA, to Schedule III. Everything else, including adult-use, stays in Schedule I.
5. **Summer 2026:** a DEA administrative law judge heard testimony from June 29 to July 15 on moving all marijuana. As of late October 2026, the recommended decision was still pending.

Because 280E covers only Schedules I and II, the April order says state medical licensees are no longer subject to it. Schedule III is still a controlled schedule, so it wouldn't make adult-use sales federally legal. Our [rescheduling explainer](/blog/cannabis-rescheduling/) tracks each step.

## What it means for Michigan shoppers today

Michigan stores still check a valid ID before every sale, for adults 21 and older or registered medical patients 18 and older. At High Society, cash works, and other payment options vary by store. And since adult-use marijuana is still Schedule I, don't travel across state lines with cannabis or bring it onto federal land.

faq.a: Because Congress put it there in 1970, and adult-use marijuana has never been moved. Schedule I covers drugs federal law classifies as having a high potential for misuse and no accepted medical use. Since April 28, 2026, marijuana under a state medical license is in Schedule III, but all other marijuana remains Schedule I.

faq.q: What did the Shafer Commission recommend?
faq.a: Its 1972 report, Marihuana: A Signal of Misunderstanding, recommended moving away from criminal penalties for personal use and discouraging use in other ways. President Nixon had appointed the commission, but his administration didn't follow its advice, and marijuana stayed in Schedule I.

faq.q: What would moving cannabis to Schedule III change?
faq.a: Mostly taxes and research. Section 280E, which blocks normal business deductions, covers only Schedules I and II, so Schedule III would lift it. It wouldn't make adult-use sales federally legal, and Michigan's own requirements for age, ID and purchase limits would stay the same.

faq.q: Is marijuana still illegal under federal law?
faq.a: Yes, for adult use. As of October 2026, adult-use marijuana remains a Schedule I controlled substance. Marijuana under a state medical license moved to Schedule III in April 2026, which keeps it federally controlled. Michigan law allows adult-use and medical sales within the state.

faq.q: Does federal law affect Michigan dispensaries?
faq.a: Yes. Federal tax treatment, banking limits and the ban on taking cannabis across state lines all trace back to scheduling. Michigan's Cannabis Regulatory Agency licenses the stores, so state law sets what you see at the counter, like ID checks and purchase limits.

claims.claim: President Nixon signed the Controlled Substances Act on October 27, 1970, as part of a larger federal drug law.
claims.evidence: "Remarks on Signing the Comprehensive Drug Abuse Prevention and Control Act of 1970, October 27, 1970"; "Public Law 91-513 (84 Stat. 1236)". LII 21 U.S.C. 812 credit: "Pub. L. 91-513, title II, sec. 202, Oct. 27, 1970".

claims.claim: Congress wrote marijuana into Schedule I in the text of the law itself.
claims.evidence: Initial schedule I(c): "(9) Lysergic acid diethylamide. (10) Marihuana."; 2024 proposed rule: "When Congress enacted the CSA in 1970, it placed marijuana in schedule I."

claims.claim: Intro: "marijuana has sat in Schedule I ... since the law was signed in 1970".
claims.fix: Outdated since April 28, 2026, when marijuana under a state medical license moved to Schedule III. Reworded: the 1970 law "put marijuana in Schedule I ... and adult-use marijuana is still there."
claims.evidence: "DATES: Effective April 28, 2026."; "any form of marijuana other than in an FDA-approved drug product or marijuana subject to a state medical marijuana license remains a schedule I controlled substance".

claims.claim: "The statute gives each schedule a three-part test: potential for misuse, accepted medical use in this country and the risk of dependence" (and a table column headed "Dependence").
claims.fix: For Schedule I the third finding is a lack of accepted safety under medical supervision, not dependence. Lead-in rewritten to say so; column renamed "Third finding" and the II-V cells now say "dependence" explicitly (IV and V relative to III and IV, as the statute words them).
claims.evidence: 812(b)(1): "(C) There is a lack of accepted safety for use of the drug or other substance under medical supervision." 812(b)(2)-(5): dependence findings.

claims.claim: Schedule table: I high/no accepted use; II high/accepted use, sometimes with severe restrictions/severe dependence; III lower than I and II/moderate or low physical or high psychological dependence; IV and V low relative to III and IV/limited dependence.
claims.fix: none (labels clarified under the previous entry)
claims.evidence: 812(b)(1)-(5) as quoted on LII.

claims.claim: The original lists put heroin and LSD in Schedule I and cocaine in Schedule II.
claims.evidence: Schedule I(b)(10) Heroin; I(c)(9) Lysergic acid diethylamide; Schedule II(a)(4) coca leaves and cocaine (with its amendment history).

claims.claim: "Changing that takes new legislation or a formal federal rescheduling process, and for five decades neither happened."
claims.fix: Legislation did change the marijuana definition (the 2018 hemp carve-out) and the April 2026 order rescheduled state-medical marijuana. Reworded: "marijuana stayed in Schedule I for more than five decades."
claims.evidence: Final rule notes the hemp definition change "had the effect of removing many products containing predominantly cannabidiol ... from control as marijuana"; effective April 28, 2026 for the Schedule III move.

claims.claim: President Nixon appointed the National Commission on Marihuana and Drug Abuse, known as the Shafer Commission after its chairman, Raymond P. Shafer.
claims.evidence: Roper: "President Richard Nixon appointed the National Commission on Marihuana and Drug Abuse, better known as the Shafer Commission". Wellcome Collection record (https://wellcomecollection.org/works/nd92929z): "with a special forward by Raymond P. Shafer, chairman", 1972.

claims.claim: The 1972 report, Marihuana: A Signal of Misunderstanding, recommended moving away from criminal penalties for personal use and discouraging use in other ways; the administration did not follow it.
claims.evidence: "The report recommended moving away from the criminalization of personal marijuana use in favor of a policy of social discouragement. Although the Nixon administration ultimately did not follow the Commission's recommendations".

claims.claim: The report landed less than a year after the President called drug abuse "public enemy number one".
claims.evidence: Report issued "On March 22, 1972" (NORML, advocacy group; date only); Nixon remarks dated June 17, 1971 (presidency.ucsb.edu): about nine months apart.

claims.claim: At the peak, hundreds of thousands of marijuana arrests a year.
claims.evidence: "In 2018 alone, there were almost 700,000 marijuana arrests".

claims.claim: "Schedule I studies need extra federal approvals, which researchers say slowed clinical work."
claims.fix: The opened sources support separate DEA research rules for Schedule I and researchers saying federal restrictions kept potent legal-market products out of studies, not specific extra approvals or slowed clinical work in general. Reworded to that.
claims.evidence: 2024 proposed rule: researchers "may be subject to different research protocols set by DEA if the research is conducted on a schedule III substance rather than a schedule I substance". Bidwell et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2020 (PMID 32520316, abstract via E-utilities): potent products "have not previously been examined in biobehavioral research studies because of federal restrictions on cannabis research".

claims.claim: Section 280E bars businesses trafficking in Schedule I or II substances from deducting normal expenses.
claims.evidence: "section 280E of the Internal Revenue Code bars businesses from claiming tax deductions for otherwise allowable expenses where the business 'consists of trafficking in controlled substances (within the meaning of schedule I and II ...)'".

claims.claim: "Banking: federal status complicates banking, one reason cash is still common at dispensaries."
claims.fix: The cash-use cause was not supported by any opened source. Reworded to what FinCEN's guidance says: banks serving cannabis businesses take on extra federal reporting duties, even for state-licensed stores.
claims.evidence: FIN-2014-G001: "Because federal law prohibits the distribution and sale of marijuana ... a financial institution is required to file a SAR on activity involving a marijuana-related business (including those duly licensed under state law)".

claims.claim: Federal law applies across state lines and on federal land.
claims.evidence: "Taking cannabis across a state line is not protected by Michigan law and remains illegal under federal law"; "Michigan's law does not protect anyone on federal land".

claims.claim: Michigan voters approved a medical program in 2008 and adult-use legalization in 2018; the Cannabis Regulatory Agency licenses the businesses.
claims.evidence: MMMA "Initiated Law 1 of 2008 ... approved Nov. 4, 2008"; MRTMA "Initiated Law 1 of 2018, effective Dec. 6, 2018"; CRA "licenses and regulates adult-use and medical marijuana businesses".

claims.claim: Hemp follows a separate federal track.
claims.evidence: The April 2026 rule "does not affect the status of hemp".

claims.claim: October 2022: the President asked for a review of marijuana's scheduling; August 2023: HHS recommended Schedule III; May 2024: DOJ proposed Schedule III.
claims.evidence: "On October 6, 2022, President Biden requested ... 'initiate the administrative process to review expeditiously how marijuana is scheduled'"; "In a letter dated August 29, 2023 ... recommended ... that marijuana be controlled in schedule III"; proposed rule published May 21, 2024 (89 FR 44597).

claims.claim: April 28, 2026: a final order moved marijuana under a state medical license and FDA-approved marijuana drugs to Schedule III; everything else, including adult-use, stays in Schedule I.
claims.evidence: "Effective April 28, 2026"; other marijuana "remains a schedule I controlled substance"; matches facts/law-facts.json us-scheduling.

claims.claim: A DEA administrative law judge heard testimony June 29 to July 15, 2026 on moving all marijuana; as of late October 2026 the recommended decision was pending.
claims.evidence: "From June 29 through July 15, DEA Chief Administrative Law Judge ... heard 11 days of testimony"; "The ALJ's recommended decision is still forthcoming" (Sept. 24, 2026); facts/law-facts.json us-rescheduling-broader: still pending as of late October 2026.

claims.claim: Because 280E covers only Schedules I and II, the April order says state medical licensees are no longer subject to it.
claims.evidence: "holders of state medical marijuana licenses will no longer be subject to the deduction disallowance imposed by Section 280E ... which applies only to businesses engaged in 'trafficking in controlled substances . . . in a schedule I or II'".

claims.claim: Schedule III is still a controlled schedule, so it would not make adult-use sales federally legal.
claims.evidence: "registrations do not authorize non-medical use"; adult-use "is still Schedule I".

claims.claim: Schedule III would change mostly taxes and research; Michigan's own age, ID and purchase-limit requirements would stay (FAQ).
claims.evidence: "section 280E would no longer serve as a statutory bar"; "different research protocols ... schedule III ... rather than a schedule I substance". State requirements come from Michigan law (facts/law-facts.json mi-au-purchase-limit).

claims.claim: Michigan stores check a valid ID before every sale, for adults 21+ or registered medical patients 18+.
claims.evidence: "Before any sale the store must check a valid driver's license or government-issued photo ID showing the buyer is 21+"; "Individuals 18 and older with a medical marijuana card can also make purchases."

claims.claim: At High Society, cash works and other payment options vary by store.
claims.evidence: "High Society accepts cash and debit cards."; credit conflicting, not stated.

claims.claim: Don't travel across state lines with cannabis or bring it onto federal land, since adult-use marijuana is still Schedule I.
claims.evidence: "transporting cannabis across state lines is prohibited under federal law" (HS); federal law applies on federal land (law-facts).

review.notes: Writer's note kept: the Egeberg 1970 'pending study' letter is not stated (no reputable page opened for it). Fact-check 2026-10-24: 26 claims checked, 5 fixed (outdated 'still Schedule I since 1970' intro; wrong 'dependence' test for Schedule I; 'five decades neither happened' ignored the 2018 hemp carve-out and the 2026 order; research and banking bullets narrowed to what opened sources say). Sources list unchanged (6, all opened or listed in law-facts, all supporting); Shafer release date and chairman checked against NORML and the Wellcome Collection record, banking against FinCEN FIN-2014-G001, research against Bidwell 2020 (in-text only, sources list is at the 6 cap).
